title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, and Profiling Playbook
author: Asha Patel
body:
Summary:
This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel and scheduling design, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, runbooks for common operational tasks, a short release-notes cadence for runtime components, and a curated list of known issues. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and anyone onboarding to the eng-serving-runtime team.

Sections:
1) Runtime Architecture (overview)

Intro:
The serving runtime is a GPU-optimized inference engine designed to support continuous batching, KV-cache aware execution, and quantization-friendly kernels. The architecture emphasizes predictable latency SLOs, cost-efficient throughput, and graceful degradation via model variants and fallback routing.

High-level components:
- Frontend API gateway: request validation, auth, rate limiting, basic per-tenant routing.
- Router & policy engine: implements routing policies (latency/cost/region/customer-tier), capacity-aware placement, and fallbacks.
- Scheduler: maps requests to worker pools, enforces batching constraints and headroom.
- Worker runtime: GPU process that performs model execution, KV cache management, and streaming responses.
- Cache & state store: Redis-backed prefix cache + S3 for large artifact storage.
- Observability pipeline: metrics -> Prometheus; traces -> Jaeger; logs -> ELK; token-level cost sampling for chargeback.

Design principles:
- Single API surface across hosted, dedicated and private deployments.
- Deterministic kernel selection using model profiles and sequence-length heuristics.
- Isolation by tenant via process-level and GPU memory partitioning.

2) Kernel selection and scheduling (detailed)

Kernel selection rules (ordered):
1. If model is quantized (INT8/4-bit) and hardware has fast INT8 kernels, prefer quantized path.
2. For sequence_length <= 64 prefer small-seq kernels optimized for low-latency.
3. For batch_size >= configured_batch_threshold prefer throughput-optimized kernels.
4. If KV-cache warm hit detected, select streaming-optimized kernels that re-use cache without full recompute.

Key scheduling components and responsibilities:
- Global scheduler (centralized): maintains global view of capacity, current queue lengths, and per-pool SLO targets. Responsible for load shedding and cross-pool fallbacks.
- Local scheduler (per-node): performs micro-batching, merges compatible requests, and decides per-GPU kernel invocation patterns.
- Admission controller: enforces per-tenant concurrency and token-rate quotas before scheduling.

Scheduling knobs (configurable):
| knob_name | default | description |
|---|---:|---|
| max_batch_size | "32" | Max requests merged into a single kernel call |
| batch_timeout_ms | "8" | Time to wait for batch fill before dispatch |
| max_concurrency_per_gpu | "64" | Soft cap for simultaneous model contexts |
| prefetch_kv_cache | "true" | Whether to pre-warm KV cache for repeated prefixes |
| throughput_priority_weight | "0.5" | Balances latency vs throughput in routing decisions |

Examples (CLI):
- Inspect scheduler state:
  $ rictl scheduler status --pool model-prod-xla
- Adjust batch timeout for a pool:
  $ rictl scheduler update-pool --pool model-prod-xla --batch-timeout-ms 6

3) Profiling playbook (how to profile and interpret results)

When to profile:
- After a model onboarding or new model-version rollout.
- When customers report latency regressions or increased tail latency.
- Periodic (monthly) perf hygiene run for critical models.

Steps to run a profiling session (quick run):
1. Reproduce workload: use the benchmarking harness to replay production traces (see section "Benchmarking suite").
2. Capture metrics: enable high-cardinality sampling for 5–10 minutes (prometheus:profiling job).
3. Enable distributed trace capture (Jaeger) for end-to-end latency.
4. Run per-GPU profiler: nvprof / Nsight Systems (preferred) or ROCm profiler on AMD nodes.

Detailed procedure (numbered):
1. Create an isolated test pool (tag: perf-profiling-YYYYMMDD).
2. Pin model to single worker and set deterministic seed for tokenization.
3. Warm-up: replay 2x expected prefix warmup to stabilize KV caches.
4. Capture 10k requests at production QPS (or scaled QPS) with trace_id enabled.
5. Run nvprof with timeline output and collection of kernel latencies:
   $ nsys profile -o profile.nsys --trace=cuda,osrt --sample=none --capture-range=nvtx --nvtx-auto 
6. Collect per-kernel histograms and export to CSV via the profiling helper script:
   $ python tools/prof/parse_nsight.py profile.nsys --out profile.csv
7. Correlate top-kernel latencies with request traces (prometheus + jaeger).
8. If tail latency is dominated by memory copies or kernel launch overhead, file a kernel-optimization ticket in the runtime backlog.

Interpreting results (common patterns):
- High kernel queueing time: indicates batch_timeout_ms too low or insufficient worker count.
- Long memcpy H2D/D2H: indicates suboptimal zero-copy paths or wrong tensor layout.
- High kernel launch overhead with small sequences: prefer small-seq fused kernels or increase micro-batch aggregation.

4) Benchmarking suite (tools and recommended workflows)

Purpose:
The benchmarking suite validates throughput and latency across model variants, quantization profiles, and hardware generations. It is used for onboarding new models, release validation, and capacity planning.

Components:
- harness/trace-replayer: replays production traffic traces with adjustable QPS and token distributions.
- harness/driver: orchestrates multiple client processes and collects end-to-end histograms and token counts.
- analyzer: aggregates results, computes p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, and cost per 1M tokens.

Canonical run (example):
1. Create a transient cluster via terraform target (see eng-infra docs).
2. Deploy model and quantization profile to target pool.
3. Run: 
   $ tools/bench/run_benchmark.sh --model redwood/llama-3-7b --quant int8 --qps 100 --duration 1800 --out results/llama3-7b-int8.json
4. Post-process: 
   $ tools/bench/analyze.py results/llama3-7b-int8.json --metrics p50,p95,p99,tokens_per_sec,cost_per_million
5. Upload results to the perf dashboard:
   $ tools/bench/upload.py results/llama3-7b-int8.json --dashboard runtime-perf

Benchmark report template (fields):
- model_name
- model_variant
- hw_gen
- quant_profile
- qps
- duration_seconds
- p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms
- tokens_per_sec
- cost_per_1M_tokens_usd
- notes

5) Runtime runbooks (operational playbooks)

Common tasks and run steps:
A) High tail latency (investigate and mitigate)
1. Check pool-level SLOs and queue depth: $ rictl scheduler status --pool <pool>
2. Check onboarding/rollout: recently deployed model? Check release notes.
3. Examine per-GPU utilization and kernel histograms (nsys output).
4. If KV cache cold starts are suspected, enable prefix cache prefetch for the pool: $ rictl scheduler update-pool --prefetch-kv-cache true
5. As emergency mitigation, enable fallback to higher-capacity model variant or increase pool size.

B) OOM on GPU during inference
1. Inspect pod/worker logs for OOM details.
2. Check model shard config and per-context memory limit.
3. Reduce max_concurrency_per_gpu or enable quantized variant.
4. If frequent, create ticket and schedule model re-quantization or change kernel with lower workspace requirements.

C) Faulty kernel causing incorrect outputs
1. Isolate traffic to the failing pool.
2. Run deterministic unit tests (tools/test/kernel_unit_tests.py) with the problematic kernel selected.
3. Roll back to last known-good kernel variant.

6) Release notes cadence (runtime components)

Policy:
- Minor runtime releases (patches) follow weekly cadence.
- Feature releases (kernel changes, scheduler changes) are gated by perf bench and profiling pass.

Release checklist (minimum):
1. Benchmarks run for affected models (baseline + candidate) and uploaded.
2. Profiling report attached with top-5 diffs.
3. Rollout plan with canary % and automated rollback condition (p99 increased > 10% or error rate > 0.1%).
4. Owner and on-call assigned for first 72 hours post-rollout.

Example short release notes entry:
- 2026-02-20: runtime v1.23.4
  - Fix: reduce kernel-launch overhead for small sequence workloads (priority models).
  - Perf: INT8 GEMM path updated for A100 and H100; ~12% tokens/sec improvement — validated on bench.
  - Note: rollback trigger if p99 latency increases > 10%.

7) Known issues (tracked, with workarounds)

- Issue: Occasional p99 spikes when batch_timeout_ms set below 5ms on high variance traffic.
  - Affects: small-seq models on H100 and A100.
  - Workaround: set batch_timeout_ms to 6-10ms or enable micro-batch aggregation.
- Issue: Memory fragmentation on long-running worker processes leading to OOM after ~72 hours in heavy multi-tenant pools.
  - Workaround: schedule periodic worker restarts via lifecycle hook (recommended: every 48h for high-load pools).
- Issue: ROCm profiler tooling produces incomplete traces for certain fused ops (known AMD driver mismatch).
  - Workaround: use CPU-side tracing and application-level histograms until driver fix applied.

8) Team wiki & onboarding checklist

Suggested onboarding steps for new runtime engineers:
1. Read this document and runtime-architecture-overview.
2. Run the canonical benchmark locally using a tiny model.
3. Pair with an on-call for two rotations.
4. Complete kernel-safe coding checklist and review ADRs under architecture-and-standards.

Useful links and commands:
- Scheduler CLI: rictl (binary in PATH for eng envs).
- Profiling tools: nsight/rocprof, tools/prof/parse_nsight.py.
- Benchmarking: tools/bench/run_benchmark.sh, tools/bench/analyze.py.
- Tracing dashboard: https://jaeger.redwood.internal/
- Perf dashboard: https://perf.redwood.internal/dashboards/runtime-perf

Appendix A: Example configuration table for a latency-sensitive pool
| field | example_value | notes |
|---|---|---|
| pool_name | "latency-critical-llm" | pool for payments and auth flows |
| max_batch_size | "8" | keep small to reduce tail |
| batch_timeout_ms | "6" | balance latency vs batching |
| max_concurrency_per_gpu | "32" | lower to limit memory pressure |
| prefetch_kv_cache | "true" | reduces cold-start p99

Appendix B: Troubleshooting checklist (compact)
- Confirm model version and recent rollouts.
- Check scheduler queue depth and pool sizing.
- Review kernel histograms and memcpy stats.
- Verify KV cache hit rate.
- If needed, perform controlled rollback.

Document maintenance:
- Owner: eng-serving-runtime (Asha Patel)
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any major runtime release.
- How to update: open a PR to this Confluence page and request review from listed reviewers.
